title: Ashura: gratitude and grief
hookLine: the fast of Musa, and the memory of Husayn
tomorrow: Auntie's hosting a mawlid. Dad isn't going. who's right?

cards: A cold bottle of water, handed to you on a hot day by a stranger, for nothing. On Ashura, in some Muslim neighborhoods, that happens on purpose: tables of water and juice by the road, free to anyone passing.
And in other homes on the same day, people are fasting, no water at all until sunset. One gives water away; one goes without it. Same day.

teach.b: Ashura holds two memories. The first is a rescue. In Sahih al-Bukhari, when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to Medina, he found Jews fasting this day.

They told him it was the day God saved Musa and the Children of Israel from their enemy, and Musa had fasted it in thanks. He answered that he, too, stood close to Musa, and he fasted it and told people to fast.

In a later report in Sahih Muslim, he said that if he lived to the next year he would fast the ninth as well, so some fast two days. Another report in Muslim says the Ashura fast wipes away the year before.
The second memory is a grief.
On Ashura, al-Tabari's history records, Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed at Karbala with members of his family, after they'd been cut off from the river's water.
Shia Muslims mourn him on this day, with gatherings, recitations and tears, and some set out water for strangers, remembering his thirst.
In Sunni practice, the day's sunna is the fast for Musa's rescue, and Husayn is honored too. Some Muslims hold both. Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: a sip of water can be a memorial.
So the day's sense is water, withheld in gratitude and given away in grief.

how: On Ashura, Sunni Muslims who keep the sunna fast the day, some adding the day before; Shia Muslims hold mourning gatherings (majalis) for Husayn and some set up stalls offering free water and drinks to passersby.

o: a Muharram day of fasting and of mourning
the night the Qur'an was first revealed
the feast at the end of the pilgrimage

games.q: one day, two memories — tap the pairs.
p: a second fast day, in Muslim
given in memory of his thirst

s: the Ashura fast is tied to Musa's rescue in a report in Bukhari
Jews in Medina told the Prophet it was the day God saved Musa; he fasted it.
Ashura means one single thing to every Muslim
it holds Musa's rescue and Husayn's death; Shia and Sunni practice weigh them differently.
fasting Ashura is only ever one day
in Muslim's report he said he'd add the ninth; some fast two days.

games.q: a friend's family sets up a water table for Ashura and asks you to help hand out drinks. you're fasting that day. what fits?
o: help hand out the water. you can fast and still give.
decline. a fasting person shouldn't even handle water.
break your fast so you can join in properly.
games.why: Ashura holds both: the fast for Musa's rescue, and water given in Husayn's memory. handing someone a drink doesn't break a fast.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or hold the one you have. Notice its weight, its coolness, the small sound it makes. Take one slow sip and let it rest on your tongue before you swallow; if you're fasting, just hold the glass.
Then set it down and stay with the two memories: a people rescued, a family left thirsty.

wordCard.voice: Ashura: a day early in Muharram, kept with a fast for Musa's rescue and in mourning for Husayn, the Prophet's grandson.

orig.note: Arabic: Ashura, the name of the day in Muharram kept with a fast and with mourning.

carryVoice: Hold this one gently: rescue and grief can share a day, and one glass of water can carry both. Four days into this part.
